# Buses and Interrupts

## Concepts

Every module boundary needs a transaction contract: who initiates requests, who returns responses, when transfers occur, and how errors and backpressure are represented. A bus adds addressing and access semantics to the data transport.

Interrupts connect peripheral events to software-visible control flow. The specification must distinguish event detection, pending state, enable state, acknowledgement, and clearing. A transient event must not disappear simply because software services it later.

## Implementation

Start from an address map and a register table. For each register, state width, reset value, access type, reserved-bit behavior, and side effects. Define how unmapped or unauthorized accesses complete.

A ready/valid adapter can demonstrate request acceptance and response buffering, but the ready/valid slice is not an implementation of a complete bus standard. Add the address, write controls, response status, and ordering rules required by the chosen protocol.

For a timer interrupt, specify whether the event is level-sensitive or latched, how software clears it, and what happens when a new event coincides with clearing. Follow the event through the SoC interrupt wiring and processor trap path.

## Hands-on Experiments

Build a register-bank model before integrating a processor. Test reset reads, ordinary writes, reserved bits, unmapped accesses, and stalled responses. Add a timer and check pending events while interrupts are disabled, acknowledgement, and simultaneous event/clear behavior.

Deliver the register map, transaction traces, and a list of implemented interrupt cases. Use these contracts to guide subsequent CORE-V Wally integration.
